patient.name: Joanne Whitfield
patient.complaint: Recurrent attacks of spinning, ringing and muffled hearing in the right ear
background: Attacks for 4 months, several a month
Drinks 5 coffees a day; enjoys salty takeaways
No ear infections, head injury or ototoxic drugs

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours plus unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness; the attack length and the ear symptoms separate it from BPPV, vestibular neuritis and acoustic neuroma.

points: Joanne, 46, has had **episodes of room-spinning vertigo** for 4 months.
Each attack lasts **2 to 3 hours**; she vomits and must lie still.
During attacks her **right ear feels full** and rings.
Her right-ear hearing is muffled, then partly recovers between attacks.

steps.lead: Joanne's symptoms come from both halves of the inner ear, hearing and balance: the picture of **endolymphatic hydrops**.
Joanne has the full **triad** (vertigo, fluctuating unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus) plus **aural fullness**.

visual.title: How long does the vertigo last?
visual.label: Joanne 2–3 hours
visual.caption: The attack length is the fastest way to sort the peripheral vertigos.

steps.lead: Joanne's attacks last **hours**, not seconds (BPPV) or days (vestibular neuritis).

steps.q: Which feature most separates Joanne's condition from vestibular neuritis?
o: Recurrent attacks with hearing loss and tinnitus
steps.r: Vestibular neuritis is a **single** attack lasting days with **no hearing loss**. Ménière's is **episodic** and hits hearing too.

points: **Head impulse test**: corrective saccade to the right.
Rinne positive both ears; **Weber lateralises to the left**.
Cranial nerves otherwise normal; no limb signs.

steps.text: In unilateral sensorineural loss, **Weber lateralises to the good ear** and Rinne stays **positive** in both ears. Conductive loss lateralises to the bad ear.
A **corrective saccade** on head impulse testing means a **peripheral** lesion. A normal head impulse test in acute vertigo is worrying for a central (stroke) cause.

steps.lead: Joanne's biggest long-term worry is her right ear: Ménière's tends to cause **progressive hearing loss** over years.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (audiometry) or 'next investigation' for asymmetric sensorineural loss (MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma). The diagnosis itself is clinical.

steps.r: Ménière's is a **clinical diagnosis** based on the history of attacks; tests support it and exclude other causes.

steps.lead: Joanne's story of repeated hour-long attacks with ear symptoms is what makes the diagnosis.
Joanne has **pure tone audiometry** to document the hearing loss in her right ear.

visual.title: Joanne's pure tone audiogram (bone conduction)
visual.caption: Right **low-frequency sensorineural** loss, typical of Ménière's. Normal hearing is under 20 dB.

steps.text: Air and bone thresholds match, so the loss is sensorineural, not conductive.

steps.title: Joanne's hearing tests
steps.text: Asymmetric sensorineural loss with a normal middle ear.

steps.lead: Joanne's loss is **asymmetric**, so she has an **MRI** of the internal auditory meatus and brain to exclude an **acoustic neuroma**.

steps.text: CT head is not the test for a cerebellopontine angle lesion: **MRI** (with gadolinium) shows a vestibular schwannoma.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' in an acute attack (prochlorperazine) or 'to prevent further attacks' (betahistine plus lifestyle); refractory disease goes to ENT for intratympanic treatment.

points: MRI is normal: no acoustic neuroma.
Joanne is in the middle of another attack: vomiting, unable to stand.
She asks for something to stop the spinning now.

steps.q: What is the best drug for Joanne's acute attack?
steps.r: **Prochlorperazine** (dopamine antagonist) for acute symptoms, as a short **1 to 2 week** course. Betahistine is for prevention.

steps.lead: Joanne cuts down **salt, caffeine and alcohol**, and takes a short course of **prochlorperazine** for the acute attack.

steps.text: Do not keep patients on vestibular sedatives long term: they **delay central compensation**. Prochlorperazine is a short course of 1 to 2 weeks.

steps.lead: Once the attack settles, Joanne starts **betahistine** to reduce how often attacks recur.

visual.title: Joanne's attacks per month
visual.caption: Fewer attacks after lifestyle change and **betahistine** started at month 1.

steps.title: Ménière's management ladder
nodes: Lifestyle: low salt, less caffeine and alcohol
Prevention: betahistine once acute symptoms settle
steps.caption: Acute relief and prevention are different drugs.

steps.lead: If Joanne's attacks kept coming despite betahistine, **ENT** would offer **intratympanic injections**; surgery is rare.

steps.text: Ménière's patients must tell the **DVLA** and stop driving if attacks come without warning. Refer to ENT to confirm the diagnosis.

steps.lead: Joanne's plan follows **NICE CKS**: confirm with ENT and audiology, treat attacks, then prevent them.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the mechanism (endolymphatic hydrops) behind the triad, or how prochlorperazine or betahistine works.

steps.lead: Joanne's inner ear has too much **endolymph**, raising pressure in the cochlear duct and the vestibular apparatus.

steps.title: From hydrops to an attack
nodes: Impaired endolymph resorption at the endolymphatic sac
Distension of cochlear duct and vestibular organs
Vertigo, low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness

steps.lead: Joanne's whole triad has **one cause**: distended membranes distort the **hair cells** of the cochlea and the vestibular organs.

steps.q: Why does the hearing loss in Ménière's begin at low frequencies?
o: The apex of the cochlea, which detects low pitch, distends first
The basal turn is damaged by ototoxins
The middle ear fills with fluid
steps.r: The **apical** cochlea (low frequencies) is the most compliant part and is affected first by hydrops. Nerve compression is acoustic neuroma.

steps.lead: Joanne's **prochlorperazine** blocks **D2** receptors and has antihistamine and anticholinergic effects that suppress the vestibular system.
Joanne's **betahistine** is thought to improve cochlear blood flow and act on **H1 and H3** receptors to calm vestibular firing.

mcq.q: What is the classic triad of Ménière's disease?
mcq.r: **Vertigo**, fluctuating unilateral **sensorineural hearing loss** and **tinnitus**, often with aural fullness.

mcq.q: How long do vertigo attacks typically last in Ménière's disease?
mcq.r: BPPV = seconds, **Ménière's = minutes to hours**, vestibular neuritis = days.

mcq.q: What does a corrective saccade on the head impulse test indicate?
mcq.r: A corrective saccade means the **peripheral** vestibulo-ocular reflex has failed.

mcq.q: What is the main long-term complication of Ménière's disease?
What is the first-line investigation in suspected Ménière's disease?
Why is MRI brain done in suspected Ménière's disease?
o: To look for middle ear fluid
mcq.r: MRI excludes other causes, especially **acoustic neuroma**; the diagnosis itself is clinical.

mcq.q: Which drug is used for an acute Ménière's attack?
mcq.r: **Prochlorperazine** for 1 to 2 weeks for acute symptoms.

mcq.q: Which drug reduces the frequency of recurrent attacks?
mcq.r: **Betahistine** is used for prevention once acute symptoms settle.

mcq.q: What is offered for severe, refractory Ménière's disease?
What is the underlying pathology of Ménière's disease?
o: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
mcq.r: **Excess endolymph** raises pressure in the cochlea and vestibular apparatus. Otoconia = BPPV.

glossary.Ménière's disease: An inner ear disorder from excess endolymph causing attacks of vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
glossary.endolymphatic hydrops: Excess endolymph fluid inside the inner ear membranes, raising pressure on the hair cells.
glossary.endolymph: Potassium-rich fluid filling the membranous labyrinth of the cochlea and vestibular system.
glossary.endolymphatic sac: Pouch draining the inner ear where endolymph is resorbed.
glossary.perilymph: Sodium-rich fluid around the membranous labyrinth, separate from endolymph.
glossary.vertigo: A false sense of movement, usually spinning, from vestibular disease.
glossary.tinnitus: Hearing a sound (ringing, roaring) with no external source.
glossary.aural fullness: A feeling of pressure or blockage in the ear.
glossary.sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing loss from the cochlea or auditory nerve rather than the outer or middle ear.
glossary.conductive hearing loss: Hearing loss from the outer or middle ear, such as wax or fluid.
glossary.nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic jerking movement of the eyes.
glossary.head impulse test: Rapid head turn while the patient fixes on your nose; a catch-up saccade shows a peripheral vestibular lesion.
glossary.corrective saccade: A quick catch-up eye movement showing the vestibulo-ocular reflex has failed.
glossary.vestibulo-ocular reflex: Reflex keeping the eyes still in space when the head moves.
glossary.Rinne's test: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction in one ear; positive (air louder) is normal or sensorineural.
glossary.Weber's test: Tuning fork on the forehead; it lateralises to the good ear in sensorineural loss and the bad ear in conductive loss.
glossary.audiometry: Hearing test plotting the quietest sounds heard at each frequency.
glossary.audiogram: The chart produced by pure tone audiometry.
glossary.dB HL: Decibels hearing level; thresholds under 20 dB are normal.
glossary.air-bone gap: Difference between air and bone thresholds; a gap means conductive loss.
glossary.tympanometry: Test of middle ear pressure and eardrum movement.
glossary.BPPV: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: seconds of vertigo on head movement from loose otoconia.
glossary.otoconia: Calcium carbonate crystals in the utricle; displaced ones cause BPPV.
glossary.vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: days of vertigo without hearing loss.
glossary.labyrinthitis: Inflammation of the inner ear causing vertigo plus hearing loss, usually after a virus.
glossary.acoustic neuroma: Benign schwannoma of the vestibulocochlear nerve causing progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus.
glossary.vestibular schwannoma: Correct name for an acoustic neuroma.
glossary.Dix-Hallpike: Positional test that provokes vertigo and nystagmus in BPPV.
glossary.Epley manoeuvre: Head repositioning manoeuvre that treats posterior canal BPPV.
glossary.prochlorperazine: Dopamine D2 antagonist anti-sickness drug used briefly for acute vertigo.
glossary.betahistine: Histamine analogue used to reduce the frequency of Ménière's attacks.
glossary.intratympanic: Given by injection through the eardrum into the middle ear.
glossary.vestibular suppressant: A drug that dampens vestibular signalling to reduce acute vertigo.
glossary.vestibular compensation: The brain's adaptation to a vestibular lesion; slowed by long-term sedatives.
glossary.hair cells: Sensory cells in the cochlea and vestibular organs that convert movement into nerve signals.
glossary.cochlea: Spiral inner ear organ for hearing.
glossary.DVLA: Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency; must be told about conditions causing sudden vertigo.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: UK primary care guidance.
